Recent US regulatory developments affecting AI server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia raise an important question:

Are our AI data-centre investments too dependent on a single technology ecosystem?

Every challenge should strengthen our next investment decision, project strategy and delivery model.

The opportunity is to rethink risk before it becomes a project-delivery or financial challenge.

Three strategic priorities:

🔹 Diversify: Explore alternative OEMs and compute platforms AMD, Intel, Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro.

🔹 Design for Flexibility: Build technology-agnostic infrastructure capable of accommodating evolving AI hardware.

🔹 Protect Investments: Secure supply chains, power, cooling capacity and regulatory compliance from day one.

To developers and investors:

Don’t build multi-billion-dollar AI infrastructure investments around a single hardware supplier.

Build flexibility into design. Diversify technology partnerships. Stress-test investment assumptions. Protect project timelines and returns.

The next competitive advantage may not simply be access to the latest GPU it may be the ability to deploy reliable, compliant and scalable compute infrastructure regardless of the hardware ecosystem.

Build for flexibility. Invest for resilience. Stay ahead of disruption.

Applied Digital signed an 18-year agreement to build and lease a massive 150 MW AIDC to a major tech giant. Facility is scheduled to begin delivering computing capacity in H1 2028.

#Money: The tech giant will pay an average of 
$$300 million per year 
$$167 per KW per month
$$2 million per megawatt, totaling 
$$5.4 billion over the 18-year base term. 

If the tech giant exercises all its renewal options (extending the lease to 33 years), Applied Digital could earn up to $12.7 billion.

#Smart #Financing: Building a facility this big costs billions upfront. Instead of footing the entire bill alone, #AppliedDigital is using a 3-step funding strategy:

1. Putting in some of its own cash, ofcourse (balance sheet equity)

2. Tapping into a $5 billion funding partnership it already set up with a giant infrastructure investor,Macquarie Asset Management

3. Using the signed 18-year lease as a guarantee to borrow the rest from banks (#ProjectFinancing) at lower interest rates, since banks know a wealthy tech giant is locked into paying rent.

Local developers (such as DCI Indonesia ,NeutraDC /Telkom Indonesia SM+ or JV with regional playersDAMAC Digital)can replicate this exact playbook by combining 4 elements:

Before pouring concrete, secure a 10-to-15+ year pre-lease with a global cloud provider (Amazon Web Services (AWS) Google Cloud Microsoft) or a major regional techfirm. A binding contract with a high-credit tenant removes the biggest risk for #lenders

Indonesian developers can form programmatic JV with global infrastructure investors / #SovereignWealthFunds (Indonesia Investment Authority (INA) GIC Brookfield ) to supply the heavy upfront equity needed for multi-hundred MW campuses

With a long-term hyperscaler lease in hand, developers can raise project-level debt from banks (DBS Bank UOB SMBC Group , orPT Bank Mandiri (Persero) Tbk. backed strictly by the future rental cash flows rather than straining the#holdco

Could Chip Compliance Become Malaysia's Next Business Opportunity? Probably A Malaysia's Technology Sovereignty Opportunity?

Nvidia has reportedly asked its server manufacturing partners to pause shipments to four Southeast Asian countries:

🇲🇾 Malaysia 🇸🇬 Singapore 🇹🇭 Thailand 🇮🇩 Indonesia

This follows new US rules that tighten where advanced AI chips can be sent and the newly set US chip license. 

Most people are asking how much this will hurt. I am asking a different question: could it also create new business?

1. The hit to the economy

In the first nine months of 2026, Malaysia approved RM123.5 billion for AI data centres, the giant computer buildings that power AI, across 86 projects.

If the chips cannot arrive on time, the builders still have bills to pay: construction, equipment and loans, with no income yet.

Banks may become more careful about lending. Local contractors and suppliers could wait longer for orders and payments.

Having a tech business is now a financial risk. 

2. The risk of chips being smuggled

When chips are in high demand but harder to buy legally, some people will try to get around the rules.

That means even honest companies may face more checks, higher costs and reputation risks.

But more checking also means more work for people who can do it.

3. Where the new business could be

Think about banks. Before they move big money, they check who you are and where the money is going. Chips may need the same kind of checks.

• Chip makers: track where each chip ends up.
• Shipping firms: keep shipments secure and traceable.
• Banks: check who they are lending to and what the chips are for.
• Data centre operators: prove who is using their computing power.
• Governments: keep an eye on technology trade.

That is work for technology or Saas firms, data companies, cybersecurity firms and compliance specialists.

4. Why Malaysia could do this

Roughly 1 in 8 of the world's chips are assembled, tested or packaged in Malaysia (about 13%).

Making chips is not the same as tracking them. But we already have the factories, engineers and shipping links to build on, so we are not starting from zero.

The bigger picture is Malaysia cannot control the supply of advanced AI chips but it could become the place the world trusts to handle them properly.

Could Malaysia become not just a chip hub, but a trusted one?

Me: "Sure, shall we discuss it together tomorrow?"

Buyer: "Just send it first. I'll call you."

- Demo completed.
- Engineers pulled into meetings.
- Special pricing approved.
- Proposal delivered before 5pm.

And then...
Emails? Nothing.
WhatsApp? Two blue ticks.
Calls? Straight to voicemail.

Funny how their internet worked perfectly when they needed the quotation.

Welcome to the ghosting pandemic in Southeast Asian enterprise sales.

To be fair, there's a cultural side to this. In Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand, people may avoid saying NO directly because they don't want to damage a relationship.

I understand that. But I'm perfectly happy hearing:
↳ We don't have the budget.
↳ We're considering another vendor.
↳ Management has changed its priorities.

That's also why, before involving my technical team, I want to establish whether there's an approved project, who makes the decision and when we'll review the proposal together.

If they're simply exploring costs, I'm happy to provide a ballpark figure.

I can respect the culture, give buyers space and make it comfortable for them to decline.

But I'm certainly not committing revenue to the board based on a buyer whose last known words were "Please send quotation ASAP."

What Is the Real Value of a WPPE Certificate?
Many people spend significant time, effort, and money to obtain a Wakil Perantara Pedagang Efek (WPPE) certification. It represents their commitment to learning, understanding capital market regulations, and preparing for a professional career in the securities industry.

But what happens after they obtain it?
Some securities companies seem reluctant to provide opportunities for WPPE holders to work in the roles they are qualified for. Instead, they are sometimes offered positions as Introducing Brokers (IBs). Others advertise equity sales positions but impose transaction targets that seem unrealistic, without considering actual market conditions.
The stock market does not always move upward. There are bullish, bearish, and sideways markets. There are also periods when investors prefer to wait rather than trade.

How can companies expect employees to achieve aggressive transaction targets without considering market realities?
Securities companies should also give their employees the opportunity to:
- Serve and maintain relationships with existing clients.
- Provide market insights and investment education.
- Build long-term client trust.
- Develop sustainable AUM and transaction growth.

A securities professional should not be measured solely by transaction volume. They should also be valued for their ability to build relationships, educate investors, and deliver meaningful services.

If securities companies want sustainable growth, they must invest in their people, not simply impose targets.

To all securities companies and hiring managers: there are many WPPE-certified professionals who genuinely want to contribute to Indonesia's capital market.

Give them a fair opportunity to prove their value.
